text.p: These are some of the main stories in Sofia newspapers today. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- Bulgaria's opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov is the new Bulgarian president who will lead the country into the next century after winning around 62 percent of the votes in the Sunday's run-off for the presidency.

-- Acknowledging Socialist party's defeat at the polls Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said on Sunday he will ask for a confidence vote from the party's Supreme Council and that a party congress could be held as early as January next year.
-- Funding talks between the Bulgarian government and an IMF mission currently in Sofia were likely to fail, well informed sources said.
-- The Russian ambassador to Bulgaria Alexander Avdeev was recalled by President Boris Yeltsin and will be replaced by Leonid Kerestedjiants.
-- Electricity and heating prices could rise by 15 percent and fuels by 14 percent in November.
-- The parliament is expected to approve the 1997 budget draft no earlier than February due to the uncertain projections for next year's macroeconomic parameters.
-- Bulgaria has to make $503 million interest payments and another $530 million principal payments on its foreign debt next year.

-- Some 73 percent of income tax revenue for 1996 and 66 percent of value added tax revenue projected under the 1996 budget have been collected so far, figures from the central bank and the finance ministry showed.

-- The Supreme Council of the ruling Socialist party is expected to hold an extraordinary meeting on November 11 to discuss the reasons for the drastic loss of votes at the presidential poll, which a senior party official described as amounting to a no-confidence vote in the party.
-- Serbia banned imports of Bulgarian meat, meat products and milk due to an outbreak of a foot-and-mouth disease.
-- Some 350 000 clients' accounts containing around 21 billion levs were blocked in state owned Economic bank after the central bank opened an insolvency suit against it last week.
